“Naturally he was entertaining, and all that, but I felt terribly let down. When I inquired about his coat of mail, he simply laughed and said England was much too cold for wearing it. Ah, Mr. Podgers has arrived! Now, Mr. Podgers, you must read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, remove your glove. Not the left one—the other.”

“Dear Gladys, I really doubt whether this is quite proper,” said the Duchess, weakly undoing a somewhat dirty kid glove.

“Nothing amusing ever is,” Lady Windermere replied. “On a fait le monde ainsi. But let me introduce you. Duchess, Mr. Podgers is my favourite cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, the Duchess of Paisley; and if you find her mountain of the moon larger than mine, I shall lose all faith in you.”

“I am certain, Gladys, that my hand contains nothing of that description,” the Duchess said solemnly.

“Your Grace is perfectly correct,” said Mr. Podgers, inspecting the small plump hand and its short, square fingers. “The mountain of the moon remains undeveloped. Your life-line, however, is admirable. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines upon the rascette! You will reach a great age, Duchess, and enjoy exceptional happiness. Ambition, quite moderate; the line of intellect, not excessive; the heart-line—”

“Do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers!” Lady Windermere exclaimed.

“Nothing would please me more,” he answered with a bow, “had the Duchess ever been so herself. Unfortunately, I perceive an enduring constancy of affection and a powerful sense of duty.”

“Please continue, Mr. Podgers,” said the Duchess, visibly gratified.

“Economy ranks by no means least among your Grace’s virtues,” he went on, sending Lady Windermere into peals of laughter.

“Economy is an excellent quality,” the Duchess observed contentedly. “When I married Paisley, he owned eleven castles and not one habitable house.”

“And now he owns twelve houses without a single castle!” cried Lady Windermere.

“Well, my dear,” the Duchess began, “I prefer—”

“Comfort,” Mr. Podgers supplied, “modern conveniences, and running hot water in every bedroom. Your Grace is entirely right. Comfort is all our civilisation has to offer.”

“You have described the Duchess wonderfully, Mr. Podgers. Now read Lady Flora.” At her smiling hostess’s nod, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and prominent shoulder-blades emerged awkwardly from behind the sofa, extending a long, bony hand with broad-tipped fingers.

“Oh, forget my hat! I want Virginia!” the young Duke cried with a laugh, and they galloped to the railway station. Mr. Otis asked the stationmaster whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but learned nothing. The stationmaster sent telegrams in both directions along the line and promised that everyone would watch carefully for her. Mr. Otis then bought the Duke a hat from a linen merchant who was just closing his shutters, and rode on to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He had been told that gypsies often visited it because of the large common nearby. They woke the village policeman, who could tell them nothing, and searched the whole common on horseback. At last they turned homeward, reaching the Chase around eleven, exhausted and nearly heartbroken. Washington and the twins waited at the gatehouse with lanterns, since the avenue was very dark. No trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught up with on Brockley meadows, but she was not among them. They explained that they had suddenly left because they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and feared arriving late. In fact, they were deeply upset to hear Virginia was missing. Grateful that Mr. Otis had allowed them to camp in his park, four had stayed to help search. The carp pond had been dragged, and the entire Chase thoroughly searched, without success. Clearly, for that night at least, Virginia remained lost to them. In deepest gloom, Mr. Otis and the boys walked toward the house, followed by the groom leading the two horses and the pony. Frightened servants stood in the hall. In the library, poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa, almost beside herself with fear and anxiety, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau de cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a sorrowful meal. Hardly anyone spoke, and even the twins, who loved their sister dearly, were frightened and subdued. When they finished, Mr. Otis sent them all to bed despite the young Duke’s pleas. He said there was nothing more to be done that night. In the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard and ask for detectives to be sent immediately.

He let her know that Frank admired her greatly and thought her beautiful and charming. With so much in his favor, she felt she ought not to judge him too severely. As Mrs. Weston said, “All young people have their little whims.”

One of his new acquaintances in Surrey was less forgiving. Generally, people throughout Donwell and Highbury judged him generously. They readily excused small faults in such a handsome young man, who smiled so often and bowed so gracefully. But one person’s critical judgment could not be softened by bows or smiles: Mr. Knightley. He heard about the incident at Hartfield and said nothing at first. Almost immediately afterward, however, Emma heard him mutter over the newspaper in his hand, “Hum! Exactly the shallow, foolish fellow I thought he was.” She was half inclined to take offense. A moment’s observation convinced her that he had spoken only to relieve his feelings, without intending to provoke her, so she let it pass.

Although Mr. and Mrs. Weston brought unwelcome news in one respect, their morning visit proved particularly well timed in another. While they were at Hartfield, something happened that made Emma want their advice. More fortunately still, the advice they gave was precisely what she wanted to hear.

This was what happened. The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years and were very decent people: friendly, generous, and unpretentious. Yet they came from humble backgrounds, made their living in trade, and were only moderately refined. When they first moved to the country, they lived quietly within their means, entertained few people, and spent little doing so. Over the past year or two, however, their income had risen considerably. Their business in London had become more profitable, and good fortune had generally favored them. As their wealth increased, so did their ambitions: they wanted a larger home and more company. They enlarged the house, hired more servants, and increased every kind of expense. By now, only the Hartfield family surpassed them in wealth and style of living. Their fondness for company and their new dining room made everyone expect dinner parties, and several gatherings, mostly for unmarried men, had already taken place. Emma could scarcely imagine them daring to invite the established leading families of Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. If they did, nothing would persuade her to attend. She regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal seem less pointed than she wished.
